anatomy.flutter: InputOtp builds a Stack of [IgnorePointer(Row of groups+separators built from InputOtpSlot), Positioned.fill(hidden EditableText)] — the painted boxes receive no events and one real EditableText covers the whole strip, exactly reproducing the package's `pointer-events: none` container plus one absolutely-positioned real <input>.
anatomy.web: OTPInput (from the input-otp package) renders the same shape: a relative container of InputOTPSlot divs plus one real, transparent, absolutely-positioned <input> stretched over the strip via containerClassName/className, as documented in input_otp.dart's own library doc citing input-otp.tsx directly.

api.flutter: InputOtp(maxLength=6, groups=[3,3], controller, initialValue, focusNode, onChanged, enabled, invalid, label, disabledReason) with an assert that groups sum to maxLength; InputOtpSlot/InputOtpSeparator are exposed as public specimen widgets for static state grids.
api.web: <OTPInput> takes maxLength plus render-prop slots; the page composes InputOTPGroup > InputOTPSlot(index) > InputOTPSeparator manually per group, reading char/hasFakeCaret/isActive off React.useContext(OTPInputContext) — the same maxLength + manual grouping shape, mirrored 1:1 in the Dart groups: List<int> parameter.

states.flutter: _isActive(index) transcribes the package's slot reducer verbatim (isFocused && selStart/selEnd logic) per the doc comment's explicit pseudocode block, and _FakeCaret uses KeyframePlayer with a discrete 0.5-cutoff opacity lookup for the 1000ms square-wave caret blink — active/inactive/invalid/disabled states all reproduced.
states.web: InputOTPSlot reads isActive/hasFakeCaret/char straight from OTPInputContext and applies data-[active=true]:z-10 data-[active=true]:border-ring data-[active=true]:ring-3 data-[active=true]:ring-ring/50 plus a `.anim-caret` div — same state matrix, package-driven rather than hand-reduced.

disabled.flutter: InputOtp.enabled (ANDed with scope) drives Disabled(disabled: !enabled, reason: widget.disabledReason ?? scope?.disabledReason, child: field) wrapping the whole strip, matching the web's has-disabled:opacity-50 on the container.
disabled.web: containerClassName carries `has-disabled:opacity-50` (input-otp.tsx:21) and className carries `disabled:cursor-not-allowed` on the underlying real input — group-level dimming plus a cursor change, both reproduced by Disabled + the enabled-gated MouseRegion cursor in InputOtp.build.

interaction.flutter: GestureDetector(onTap: () => _editableKey.currentState?.requestKeyboard()) over the whole strip plus keyboardType: TextInputType.number, autofillHints: [AutofillHints.oneTimeCode], and LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter(maxLength) reproduce inputMode="numeric"/autoComplete="one-time-code"/maxLength from the package, and _onFocusChanged sets the selection range to mirror the package's onFocus handler so the active box lands correctly.
interaction.web: The input-otp package wires numeric keyboard mode, one-time-code autofill, length limiting, and the onFocus selection-range logic (setSelectionRange(min(len,max-1), len)) that input_otp.dart's doc comment quotes directly as the source it ported from.

semantics.flutter: Semantics(textField: true, label:, hint:, enabled:, validationResult: invalid ? invalid : none) is applied once to the whole strip, and InputOtpSeparator wraps its Icon in ExcludeSemantics with a comment explaining a dash announced mid-code is noise (inputs-map §7.2) — the same reasoning the web's role="separator" choice reflects, but not the same mechanism.
semantics.web: InputOTPSeparator carries an explicit role="separator" on a real DOM node (input-otp.tsx:79) rather than excluding it from the tree outright; a screen reader can still encounter role="separator" as a landmark even though it announces no content, which is a different (if arguably equivalent) accessibility surface than Flutter's ExcludeSemantics removing the node entirely.
semantics.note: input_otp.dart's own doc comment explains the choice directly: "role=\"separator\" has no Flutter counterpart worth inventing, and a dash announced between two halves of a code is noise (inputs-map §7.2)". Excluding the separator glyph from the accessibility tree entirely is the idiomatic Flutter answer to a decorative role that announces no content on the web either — the practical screen-reader experience converges (nothing useful is ever read for the dash on either platform), so this is recorded as a correct, deliberate platform difference rather than a missing feature.
